title: Detection Strategy for Scheduled Transfer and Recurrent Exfiltration Patterns
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for Scheduled Transfer and Recurrent E...
summary: This detection strategy focuses on data leaving the environment on a repeating timetable, matching the scheduled transfer technique where an adversary uses task schedulers or cron to move collected files at fixed intervals. The distinguishing evidence is not the volume of any single transfer but the rhythm: outbound sessions that recur at nearly the same interval from the same host with similar payload sizes, plus the local artefact that created the schedule. The telemetry that makes this possible is scheduled task creation and modification events, cron or systemd timer file writes on Linux, network flow records with timestamps and byte counts, and cloud storage upload audit logs. It fails most often because software update agents, monitoring checks and backup jobs are exactly this shape, so without an allow list of known periodic jobs the rule describes your own automation better than the attacker.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for data that leaves your network on a fixed timetable. Examples are every ten minutes, or every night at one o'clock. It also checks for the scheduling entry that created that timetable. The alert means a repeating transfer exists that nobody has approved.
beginner.whyItMatters: A steady timetable is a strong sign that a program, not a person, is sending data. People are irregular; scripts are punctual. Finding the schedule early lets you stop the flow and find the program that made it. It also gives you a clear artefact to remove from the computer. Without this detection, slow theft can continue for months because each single transfer looks small and ordinary.
howItWorks: Endpoint monitoring records new or changed scheduled task entries, cron files and system timer units.
Network devices record every outbound session with the time and the number of bytes sent.
Both feeds arrive at the security monitoring platform with the host name and account.
The rule looks for outbound sessions from one host that repeat at a similar interval with similar sizes.
It then looks for a scheduled job or timer on that same host created shortly before the pattern began.
Matching a new schedule with a new repeating transfer raises a high confidence alert for review.
beginner.example: Think of a night watchman who checks the same door at the same minute every hour. The log looks boring because it repeats. Now a second person starts checking the back gate every ten minutes. No manager scheduled that round, so the pattern itself is the clue. This detection reads the round sheet.
takeaways: Repeating on a regular interval is the signature of automated transfer.
Always pair a network pattern with the local schedule that could produce it.
Your own update and backup jobs look identical, so list them before you tune thresholds.

objectives: Describe how interval regularity distinguishes scheduled transfer from human activity.
Identify the local scheduling artefacts used on Windows, Linux and macOS.
Correlate a new schedule entry with the first appearance of a repeating outbound transfer.
Build an inventory of approved periodic jobs and their destinations.
Explain the coverage gaps when endpoint and network clocks are not synchronised.
dataSources: Windows Security scheduled task creation and modification events including task name, author and action path
Windows Security process creation events for the task scheduler service starting a process with a script interpreter
Linux audit records for writes to cron directories and systemd timer unit files with the writing process
Network flow or proxy records with session start time, destination and bytes sent per session
Cloud storage upload audit logs showing repeated uploads by one identity at regular intervals
logic: The pattern is an outbound session from one internal host repeating at a low variance interval, such as every ten or sixty minutes, with similar payload sizes to the same destination, especially a destination with no prior history, combined with a newly created or modified scheduled job, cron entry or timer on that host within the preceding hours. The fields to correlate are the task or unit name and its author or creating process, the host and account that own the job, the destination address or bucket, the inter session interval computed from flow timestamps, and the byte counts. The benign case is patch, backup, telemetry and monitoring jobs that belong to a known tool with a documented destination; the malicious case is a job whose action is a script interpreter with a long obfuscated command line, created by a non administrative process, pointing at a destination your estate has never used.
pseudoQuery:
# title: New Scheduled Job Correlated with Repeating Outbound Transfer
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: security
# detection:
#   selection_task:
#     event_id: 4698
#   selection_action:
#     task_action|contains:
#       - 'powershell'
#       - 'cmd.exe /c'
#       - 'curl'
#       - 'certutil'
#   filter_approved:
#     task_author|endswith: '$@corp.example'
#   condition: selection_task and selection_action and not filter_approved
# level: high
falsePositives: Patch management and inventory agents that phone home on a fixed polling interval to a vendor service
Database administrators who schedule nightly extract jobs that upload result files to a reporting share
Monitoring checks that run every five minutes from a management server to a central collector
Developer laptops running a build cache sync task at a regular interval against an approved artifact repository
tuningNotes: Inventory every scheduled job on a sample of hosts first, and record the executable, the action path, the author and the destination, then allow list by those four attributes rather than by task name, because names repeat. Filter interpreter based actions whose full command line matches a known management framework, and suppress jobs created by your configuration management service account. Scope the network half of the rule to destinations outside your own address space so internal transfers do not fire. The coverage you give up is a malicious job that hides inside an approved task name with a modified action, so keep a change detection alert on approved tasks and review modifications weekly.
